spending.how: Each board's audited expenses for the school year (all sources of money, not only the province's), divided by its students that year. Instruction is ECS plus grades 1 to 12; buildings is operations and maintenance. Capital (new schools) is not an operating expense.

approvals.how: School projects each provincial budget approves (new, replacement, modernization, addition, charter), from the approved school capital lists (Budget 2025 on; the 2024 list is laid out differently and mixes new approvals with projects moving to their next stage, so it is not counted), counted by the community the list gives. Most are approved for planning or design first, so an approval is not yet a building. Growth: students in each city's two city boards over as many school years as budgets counted.

grants.how: Each board's funding profile for the coming school year, line by line, divided by its students in the latest enrolment file (for scale: the profile counts projected students).

factors.factor: Fewer students per resident in Calgary
factors.what: Calgary has fewer school-age children per resident than the rest of Alberta, so the same tax per resident is more per student. Compare tax per resident (residents) with tax per student before calling a gap unfair.

The requisition includes non-residential property. Calgary's offices and shops pay part of it; in many rural municipalities oil, gas and pipeline property pays most of it, so some rural places pay far more per resident than Calgary (municipalities_per_resident).

Until 2024/25 the province funded boards on a weighted moving average of enrolment (20% the year before, 30% this year, 50% next year's projection), which pays fast-growing boards such as Calgary's for fewer students than they have; from 2025/26 it is 30% last year and 70% the projection, a smaller lag. A supplemental growth grant pays part of the gap. Set funding per student beside each board's growth.

Funding per student differs by need, not by city: rural boards get transportation, geographic and small-school money; boards with many newcomers get English as an additional language and refugee grants; specialized learning, First Nations, Métis and Inuit, and socio-economic status grants follow students (grants).

New schools are approved in each budget (approvals) and built over several years; maintenance and renewal money (IMR and CMR) is separate from operating funding. Operations and maintenance spending per student is in spending.

factors.factor: Money that does not pass through the boards
factors.what: The province pays teachers' pension costs directly, and funds private schools (about 70% of a public student's base) and home education outside these board figures; Calgary has many private-school students, so the board figures understate the money that reaches Calgary's students.
Boards charge fees (transportation, lunch supervision, materials) that differ by board; they are in the audited revenues, not in provincial funding.

Requisitions are calendar years, enrolment and funding school years; board students include some living outside the city; the 2027 standard rate changes the rate but not the fact that more valuable property pays more.

rates.note: From 2027 one education tax rate applies in every municipality, frozen for three years (announced 30 October 2026), with a one-time transition credit where the new rate is higher than the old local rate. Until 2026 each municipality had its own rate, set from its equalized assessment.
